slot.brief: Give two octahedral complexes of the same metal ion but different ligands from opposite ends of the spectrochemical series; ask which is high-spin and compare unpaired electrons.

stem: For the octahedral complexes $[\text{FeF}_6]^{4-}$ and $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$, which statement correctly compares their spin states and numbers of unpaired electrons?
options: $[\text{FeF}_6]^{4-}$ is low-spin with 0 unpaired electrons; $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ is high-spin with 4.
$[\text{FeF}_6]^{4-}$ is high-spin with 2 unpaired electrons; $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ is low-spin with 0.
$[\text{FeF}_6]^{4-}$ is high-spin with 4 unpaired electrons; $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ is low-spin with 0.
Both complexes are high-spin, with 4 unpaired electrons in each.

verdicts.working: In both complexes, Fe is +2 (d⁶). F⁻ gives high-spin t₂g⁴e_g² with 4 unpaired electrons; CN⁻ gives low-spin t₂g⁶ with 0.

working:
$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is $d^6$ in both complexes.
$\text{F}^-$ is weak-field: high-spin $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$, 4 unpaired electrons.
$\text{CN}^-$ is strong-field: low-spin $t_{2g}^6$, 0 unpaired electrons.

Independent check: In both complexes, Fe is +2 (d⁶). F⁻ gives high-spin t₂g⁴e_g² with 4 unpaired electrons; CN⁻ gives low-spin t₂g⁶ with 0.
solution: In both complexes, Fe is in the $+2$ oxidation state, so it has a $d^6$ configuration. $F^-$ is weak-field, giving high-spin $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$ with 4 unpaired electrons; $CN^-$ is strong-field, giving low-spin $t_{2g}^6$ with 0 unpaired electrons.
